power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background Digital platforms provide contexts for both normative adolescent sexual exploration and potential victimization.
We lack understanding of the diversity of experiences adolescents encounter, and importantly, and how they subjectively appraise them.
How a young person subjectively perceives an event may impact associations with health.

Methods This preregistered study used population-based self-report data from 3,675 adolescents aged 12-16 years to examine the prevalence of different online sexual experiences and violations, ranging from sharing sexual content to having nude images spread on social media.

Additionally, the study probes several measures of subjective appraisals, including how distressing experiences were, regret and assessments of the extent to which one felt one was forced or tricked into the experience.

Generalized linear models were used to examine associations between cumulative exposure to online sexual experiences and violations and mental health symptoms (Hopkins Symptom Checklist), somatic symptoms (Children's Somatic Symptoms Inventory), and current and peak subjective distress related to these experiences.
Regret was examined as a potential moderator.
Logistic regression examined the history of offline sexual abuse by an adult as a risk factor.
2 Results By age 16, 49% of adolescents reported at least one online sexual experience or violation.
Greater cumulative exposure was associated with more mental and somatic symptoms and higher current and peak subjective distress.

Associations with symptoms remained even when accounting for symptoms from two years prior, family affluence, removing most severe items, and excluding participants reporting being coerced or tricked into the experience.
Regret did not moderate exposure -subjective distress associations.
Offline sexual abuse by an adult substantially increased the odds of having online sexual experiences or violations.
Girls reported more coercion and subjective distress related to online sexual experiences, although boys were less likely to provide data on these measures.

Conclusions Digital contexts should be recognized as important developmental arenas in which adolescents navigate sexuality and intimacy, and where normative exploratory processes and potential risks co-occur.

Future research should examine the socio-contextual factors that may render some online sexual experiences detrimental to health, informing efforts to create safer digital spaces that support adolescents' exploration while protecting them from harm.

Digital technologies have become embedded in the everyday lives of children and adolescents (Ofcom, 2025), shaping how young people form identities, explore sexuality, and build relationships (Maes et al., 2022; Nesi et al., 2020).

text.text: Developmental psychologists increasingly argue that online environments should therefore be treated as central developmental contexts in which key social and psychological processes unfold (Nesi et al., 2020).

text.text: Like traditional physical contexts in which adolescents interact with peers, such as schools, leisure activities, and other offline social settings, digital environments can provide opportunities for connection, self-expression, help-seeking, and exploration.
At the same time, digital environments have unique affordances, including permanence, public visibility and disseminability.
The content of online interactions can also be rapidly shared with large numbers of other people, thereby making harmful experiences more difficult to escape or contain.
Quantifiable feedback and constant connectivity may also introduce risks that undermine well-being and mental health (Keles et al., 2020; Nesi et al., 2018; Orben et al., 2024).

text.text: Studying online experiences in relation to mental and somatic health is particularly important in adolescence.
This developmental period is marked by substantial physical and psychological changes, as well as social reorientation toward peers (Nelson et al., 2005).
text.formatted: This developmental period is marked by substantial physical and psychological changes, as well as social reorientation toward peers <ref type="bibr">(Nelson et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Major developmental changes include heightened sensitivity to peer evaluation and rejection (Sebastian et al., 2010; Sommerville, 2013), increased need for social belonging (Blakemore & Mills, 2014), and peer influence on behavior, including risk-taking (Simons-Morton et al., 2011 , 2019).

text.text: These developmentally normative aspects of adolescence likely interact with the online contexts that adolescents navigate, shaping both the kinds of experiences they encounter and how they respond to them.

For example, just as adolescents may be prone to risk-taking in offline peer settings (Simons-Morton et al., 2011), similar processes may occur in online environments, but in ways that are shaped by the specific affordances of digital platforms.

text.text: Given that many mental health problems emerge in adolescence, and that prevention is particularly critical around the time of onset (Solmi et al., 2022), it is important to understand how adverse experiences that arise in online contexts may shape adolescent mental health.

text.text: Although changing cultural attitudes toward mental health, including reduced stigma and greater willingness to report symptoms, may influence prevalences of mental health symptoms, available evidence suggests that they cannot fully account for the observed decline in adolescent mental health over the past decade (McElroy et al., 2023).

text.text: This has sparked debate about whether increased engagement with digital platforms among young people may contribute causally to poorer adolescent mental health (Coyne et al., 2020; Twenge et al., 2018).

text.text: However, despite the intuitive appeal of this idea, empirical support remains mixed, in part because of methodological shortcomings, including a lack of specificity.

Much research has, for example, relied on broad measures such as time spent online (Riehm et al., 2019; Twenge et al., 2018), which may obscure the heterogeneity of experiences young people have, as well as the heterogeneity of responses these experiences may evoke.

text.text: Just as decades of research have explored nuances in traditional offline developmental contexts, developmental psychology must now also examine the nuances of the online developmental contexts that young people inhabit today.

Turning attention to sexual experiences adolescents may encounter in online development contexts, these can vary from consensual normative experiences to sexual abuse (Döring, 2014; Wolak et al., 2008).

text.text: Although emerging research suggests that online sexual abuse is associated with health outcomes comparable to those linked to offline sexual abuse (Jonsson et al., 2019), abuse occurring in online contexts is still sometimes minimized or underestimated by professionals (Hamilton-Giachritsis et al., 2017), highlighting the need for further research on its associations with mental and somatic health outcomes.

text.text: Studying links between broad measures such as time spend on digital platforms and health outcomes (e.g. Riehm et al., 2019) yield thought-provoking findings, but may not provide insights into the specific types of experiences young individuals encounter and importantly, how they subjectively experience them.

text.text: Not all experiences in digital settings are inherently negative.
Specific affordances of digital platforms, such as anonymity and accessibility, may allow adolescents to explore sexuality and intimacy and to seek information and support (Suto et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Specific affordances of digital platforms, such as anonymity and accessibility, may allow adolescents to explore sexuality and intimacy and to seek information and support <ref type="bibr">(Suto et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: As such, by creating opportunities for connection, exploration, and support, digital platforms may facilitate normative developmental processes.
However, these same affordances may also increase the risk of adverse experiences, including sexual harassment, solicitation, and abuse.

The online context can lower young people's inhibitions and create a false sense of safety, while accessibility and affordability may extend perpetrators' reach both geographically, by expanding the pool of potential victims beyond immediate offline environments, and temporally, by enabling contact late into the night in ways that may deepen influence and preserve secrecy (Hamilton-Giachritsis et al., 2017).

text.text: Permanence, whereby sexual content may be difficult to remove from the internet, and the ease and speed of potential dissemination are additional features that may influence how harmful an online sexual experience can become (Page et al., 2025; Salter et al., 2023).

text.text: Online context can thus promote developmental processes that unfold in adolescence but also pose numerous risks.

A parallel distinction has characterized research on adolescent sexual development more broadly: a longstanding emphasis on sexual risks and adverse outcomes has been complemented by research examining sexuality as a normative developmental process with positive qualities and consequences. Tolman and McClelland (2011) called for integrating these perspectives rather than treating positive sexuality and risk management as opposing domains.

text.text: From this perspective, adolescent sexual development involves learning both how to pursue wanted, positive sexual experiences and how to recognize, negotiate, and manage potential risks.
This integrated perspective should also inform research on sexual experiences in online developmental contexts, where opportunities for exploration and connection coexist with potential risks.

Additionally, it is increasingly recognized that, in order to understand how adverse events affect children's development, research must also consider children's subjective appraisals (Pollak & Smith, 2021).

text.text: Seemingly similar events may be experienced as minimally or highly distressing depending on the child's individual characteristics and contextual factors, and subjective experience of the seemingly adverse event is a predictor of health outcomes (Ferschmann et al., 2026).

text.text: It is thus important not only to examine correlates of event-based characteristics (what happened) but also inquire into how they were experienced by the young person (was it distressing for the person).

The present study aims to address these knowledge gaps by moving beyond broad indicators of digital engagement by examining adolescents' experiences with range of online sexual experiences, alongside their subjective appraisals of those experiences.
In addition to subjective distress related to how sexual experiences in online settings are perceived by adolescents, this study will also examine regret.
Examining regret is not intended to place responsibility on adolescents for negative outcomes or harms that may arise following an interaction.

Rather, regret may be informative in understanding the gray zone between consensual and non-consensual sexual experiences by capturing how individuals interpret an experience after it has taken place (Akre et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Rather, regret may be informative in understanding the gray zone between consensual and non-consensual sexual experiences by capturing how individuals interpret an experience after it has taken place <ref type="bibr">(Akre et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: This may be particularly relevant in online settings, where an initially voluntary interaction can later take on a different meaning, for example if private sexual content is shared beyond the intended recipient.
Greater insight into adolescents' subjective appraisals as they navigate sexual experiences in online contexts is therefore critical for understanding associations with mental and somatic health.
Using cross-sectional data from a large population-based sample of Norwegian adolescents aged 12-16 years, the present preregistered study had several aims.

First, we aimed to map the range of sexual experiences that adolescents encounter in online settings, including both voluntary behaviors (e.g., sending sexual content) and non-consensual acts (e.g., receiving unwanted sexual content or image-based abuse).
We included this range of experiences as, particularly among older adolescents, the boundaries between developmentally normative voluntary exploration and abuse can be blurry.
Second, we will explore associations between these sexual experiences and violations in online settings and mental and somatic symptoms.
Third, we aimed to investigate subjective appraisals of these online experiences, including perceived distress and subsequent regret.

If regret reflects a retrospective appraisal of the adverse experience, including the perception that one's own actions may have contributed to what occurred (van Dijk & Zeelenberg, 2002), then higher levels regret may also intensify retrospective subjective distress related to what happened.

text.text: Finally, we examined whether prior exposure to offline sexual abuse by an adult is associated with increased odds of reporting sexual experiences and violations in online settings.

This expectation is consistent with the polyvictimization framework, which suggests that children exposed to one form of victimization are at increased risk of experiencing other forms of victimization across contexts (Finkelhor et al., 2007).
text.formatted: This expectation is consistent with the polyvictimization framework, which suggests that children exposed to one form of victimization are at increased risk of experiencing other forms of victimization across contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Finkelhor et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Our preregistered hypotheses were formulated as follows: H1: Higher cumulative exposure to sexual experiences and violations in online settings will be associated with poorer mental and somatic health.
H2: Higher cumulative exposure to sexual experiences and violations in online settings will be associated with higher levels of subjective distress related to these experiences.
H3: the association between sexual experiences and violations in online settings and subjective distress will be stronger in individuals with higher levels of regret.
H4: exposure to sexual abuse in offline settings committed by an adult will increase the odds of having sexual experiences or being exposed to sexual violations in online settings.

A unique feature of this study is that participation did not require parental consent, enabled by the independent consent regulation introduced in 2017 (Health Research Act § 17), which permits such consent from the age of 12 under specific conditions.

The regulation is intended for exceptional circumstances and includes, among other conditions, situations in which parental consent could compromise participation or disclosure because the research concerns information that parents may have an interest in concealing (e.g., violence, neglect, or abuse), requirements that the societal value of the research clearly outweigh potential burdens to participants, and obligations for researchers to have procedures in place for responding if participation reveals a need for health care or other support.

The first question assessed current subjective distress: 'On a scale from 1 to 10, how much does this bother you right now?'
The second question measured peak subjective distress: 'On a scale from 1 to 10, how much has this bothered you at its worst?'

The same model was extended with an interaction term consisting of exposure to online sexual experiences and violations and level of self-reported regret, to test whether associations between exposure to online sexual experiences and violations and subjective distress would be stronger in in individuals with higher levels of regret (hypothesis 3).

text.text: This study aimed to move beyond broad indicators of young people's digital engagement, such as time spent online, by examining specific online sexual experiences and violations and their associations with somatic and mental health symptoms.
Importantly, the study sought to increase specificity further by moving beyond mere event descriptions to include measures of subjective appraisals of these experiences.
Greater exposure to online sexual experiences and violations was associated with more mental and somatic health symptoms.
Greater exposure was also linked to more negative subjective appraisals regarding these experiences.
This latter association was not moderated by regret.
Having previously experienced sexual abuse by an adult in offline settings was linked to substantial increased odds of reporting sexual experiences and violations in online settings.

With nearly half of the population-based sample reporting some form of sexual experiences or violations in online settings by age 16, the present findings highlight that digital platforms constitute important developmental contexts where adolescents navigate sexuality, intimacy, vulnerability and potential harm.
Hypothesis 1 was supported: the association between sexual experiences and violations in online settings and higher levels of mental and somatic symptoms.

The association with mental symptoms is consistent with studies showing that adolescents whose sexual images have been shared without their consent report higher levels of depression, lower self-esteem, suicidality, and other mental health difficulties (Pampati et al., 2020; Schmidt et al., 2024; Sciacca et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The association with mental symptoms is consistent with studies showing that adolescents whose sexual images have been shared without their consent report higher levels of depression, lower self-esteem, suicidality, and other mental health difficulties <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Pampati et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Schmidt et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Sciacca et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The association with somatic symptoms is also in line with the broader literature on sexual victimization.

Prospective and longitudinal studies have found that sexual abuse and assault during childhood or adolescence are associated with subsequent headaches, abdominal pain, nausea, and other functional somatic symptoms (Bonvanie et al., 2015; Casanovas et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Prospective and longitudinal studies have found that sexual abuse and assault during childhood or adolescence are associated with subsequent headaches, abdominal pain, nausea, and other functional somatic symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Bonvanie et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Casanovas et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, such associations do not appear to be limited to abuse perpetrated by adults.

Sexual harassment by peers, including physical sexual harassment and sexual name-calling, has also been prospectively associated with somatic and depressive symptoms among adolescents (Dahlqvist et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Sexual harassment by peers, including physical sexual harassment and sexual name-calling, has also been prospectively associated with somatic and depressive symptoms among adolescents <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Dahlqvist et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Although the experiences included in the present cumulative score varied in their nature and severity, several represented clear violations of sexual autonomy, privacy, and consent, such as being made to perform sexual acts while being watched or having nude images or videos distributed on social media.

Such violations may evoke shame, fear of further dissemination, loss of control, and difficulties in interpersonal relationships, which may contribute to sustained distress and potentially manifest in both psychological and somatic symptoms (Hellevik et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Such violations may evoke shame, fear of further dissemination, loss of control, and difficulties in interpersonal relationships, which may contribute to sustained distress and potentially manifest in both psychological and somatic symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Hellevik et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: More notable, however, was that the associations with both mental and somatic symptoms remained significant even after i) removing the most clearly abusive or coercive items (being made to perform sexual acts while being watched or having one's nude images or videos being spread on social media), and ii) excluding adolescents who specifically reported being tricked, threatened or forced into any of the measured sexual experiences in online context.
This suggests that the association is not only driven by the most overtly abusive or coercive experiences.

This finding may be considered in light of research on normative sexual development, which suggests that the implications of sexual experiences for health and well-being depend not only on the nature of the experience itself, but also on how it is perceived and evaluated within its developmental and socio-cultural context.

Youth sexual activity has been associated with both poorer mental health and greater well-being, with associations varying according to factors such as peer norms (for example whether an experience is age-appropriate), partner context (e.g. romantic partner or not), and parental attitudes toward adolescent sexuality (Meier, 2007; Vasilenko, 2017; Vrangalova & Savin-Williams, 2011).
text.formatted: Youth sexual activity has been associated with both poorer mental health and greater well-being, with associations varying according to factors such as peer norms (for example whether an experience is age-appropriate), partner context (e.g. romantic partner or not), and parental attitudes toward adolescent sexuality <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Meier, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Vasilenko, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Vrangalova & Savin-Williams, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Pre-existing individuallevel characteristics may also be of importance.

Longitudinal studies suggest that depressive symptoms and other indicators of poor psychological health may predict subsequent sexual harassment victimization (Dahlqvist et al., 2016; Skoog & Kapetanovic, 2021).
text.formatted: Longitudinal studies suggest that depressive symptoms and other indicators of poor psychological health may predict subsequent sexual harassment victimization <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Dahlqvist et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Skoog & Kapetanovic, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: These perspectives may also be relevant to understanding sexual experiences and violations in online settings.

As with offline sexual experiences, their implications for health may depend on the developmental, interpersonal, and socio-cultural context in which they occur and how they are perceived by the young person.

Relevant factors may include whether the experience is perceived as normative among peers, the relationship to the person involved, and the adolescent's age and developmental stage at the time of the experience.
Although the present study accounted for age at assessment, we could not examine age at onset of the different experiences due to substantial missing data on the age of onset variable.
Pre-existing individual differences in mental and somatic health may also play a role.

While our study could not establish temporal or reciprocal associations, associations with mental and somatic symptoms remained significant after accounting for pre-existing differences in mental and somatic health, suggesting that they were not solely driven by poorer health preceding these experiences.
In online settings, the relational context and subjective appraisal of an experience may be particularly important.

For example, receiving sexual content from a same-age romantic partner may be perceived as positive and age-appropriate, whereas receiving similar content unsolicited from an unknown person may evoke discomfort or uncertainty.
Qualitative research suggests that adolescents may experience unsolicited nude images with discomfort, feel pressure to reciprocate, or find it difficult to say no (Mishna et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Qualitative research suggests that adolescents may experience unsolicited nude images with discomfort, feel pressure to reciprocate, or find it difficult to say no <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Mishna et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This variation in how online sexual experiences can be perceived may help explain why associations with mental and somatic symptoms remained even after the most clearly coercive or abusive experiences were removed from the cumulative exposure score.

The remaining experiences may encompass both exploratory behaviors that form part of normative sexual development and experiences that are ambiguous, unwanted, uncomfortable, or otherwise negatively perceived.

Thus, the association between the trimmed cumulative exposure score and higher symptom levels may partly reflect differences in the context and subjective meaning of these experiences that were not captured by the exposure measure itself.

Hypothesis 2 was supported: greater exposure to online sexual experiences and violations was associated with higher levels of both peak and current subjective distress when thinking about what happened.
As with the previous hypothesis, this may suggest that with increasing numbers of online sexual experiences, the probability of experiencing subjectively distressing events increases.
What remains a critical question is which factors determine whether an event is appraised retrospectively as distressing or not.
In this study, we examined regret as one such factor.
Hypothesis 3, stating that the association between greater exposure and subjective distress in response to what happened, would be stronger in individuals who reported regret, was not supported.
The lack of moderation may indicate that regret, at least as measured in this study, captures only a limited aspect of adolescents' retrospective appraisal of how distressing the experience was.

Experimental research on offline sexual scenarios suggest that perceived distress is shaped by multiple factors including consent, wantedness and pleasure (Hills et al., 2020), and future studies should explore these factors in the context on online sexual experiences.
text.formatted: Experimental research on offline sexual scenarios suggest that perceived distress is shaped by multiple factors including consent, wantedness and pleasure <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hills et al., 2020)</ref>, and future studies should explore these factors in the context on online sexual experiences.

text.text: Additionally, the regret item in our study was framed as "Have you ever regretted having done this", thereby foregrounding the adolescent's own actions.
It is possible that other factors, that instead direct attention to "what the other person did" may be another useful avenue to pursue.
Examples of such factors are invasiveness and exploitativeness, introduced by the 3-D theory (Emery et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Examples of such factors are invasiveness and exploitativeness, introduced by the 3-D theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Emery et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Invasiveness refers to transgressions of normative boundaries around the body or the (sexual) self, while exploitativeness refers to being instrumentally used by another person for their own purposes or self-gratification.
These constructs may be especially relevant in online settings, where affordances of digital platforms can alter the meaning and consequences of an experience after it has taken place.
For example, sharing sexual content with someone one is romantically interested in may initially be consensual and pleasurable.
Unlike many offline sexual interactions, digital sexual content can be screenshotted, redistributed, or recontextualized without the sender's knowledge.
If the recipient later shares the content with peers to enhance his social status, the young person may retrospectively appraise the experience as invasive and exploitative.

In other words, future research should thoroughly explore factors that impact the intensity of subjective distress experienced, which digital affordances enable these factors and how such risks can be limited.
Girls had higher odds of exposure to sexual experiences and violation settings in an online context.

This finding is consistent with gendered patterns documented in offline adolescent contexts, where girls tend to report more unwanted sexual attention and harassment, as well as sexual violence (Kaltiala, 2022; Stoltenborgh et al., 2011).
text.formatted: This finding is consistent with gendered patterns documented in offline adolescent contexts, where girls tend to report more unwanted sexual attention and harassment, as well as sexual violence <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Kaltiala, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Stoltenborgh et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Literature regarding gender differences in online settings is more mixed.
Some studies indicate that girls are more likely than boys to experience a wide range of sexual encounters and violations in online settings (Finkelhor et al., 2024; Gámez-Guadix et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Some studies indicate that girls are more likely than boys to experience a wide range of sexual encounters and violations in online settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Finkelhor et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Gámez-Guadix et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, a recent large meta-analysis of representative surveys including data from 123 countries found no major gender differences in online sexual victimization (Fry et al., 2025), suggesting that patterns of risk may differ from those observed in traditional offline settings.
text.formatted: However, a recent large meta-analysis of representative surveys including data from 123 countries found no major gender differences in online sexual victimization <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Fry et al., 2025)</ref>, suggesting that patterns of risk may differ from those observed in traditional offline settings.

text.text: Similarly, a survey on online sexual child sexual solicitation and abuse among young adults found higher rates among women for some experiences, particularly unwanted sexualized interactions, although effect sizes were small, whereas other experiences were reported at similar rates by men and women (Chauviré-Geib et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Similarly, a survey on online sexual child sexual solicitation and abuse among young adults found higher rates among women for some experiences, particularly unwanted sexualized interactions, although effect sizes were small, whereas other experiences were reported at similar rates by men and women <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Chauviré-Geib et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This is partly in line with our findings, which indicate girls encounter higher rates of online sexual experiences and violations, although when explored at item-level, effect sizes were mostly small.

However, in our study, gender was associated with perceptions of being forced or tricked into the experience and both measures of subjective distress related to that experience with small-to-moderate and moderate effect sizes.
There are several possible explanations for these observed differences.
First, it is possible that girls encounter experiences in online settings that genuinely involve more coercion or discomfort.
Alternatively, boys may be less willing to disclose sexually abusive experiences, as documented in offline settings (Hietamäki et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Alternatively, boys may be less willing to disclose sexually abusive experiences, as documented in offline settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Hietamäki et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: That may help explain why boys in our sample were less likely to provide complete data on sexual experiences and violations and why, among exposed youth, boys were less likely than girls to provide ratings of subjective distress related to online experiences.
Research on sexual trauma in men shows that disclosure and labeling oneself as a victim may violate traditional masculine norms of being strong and invulnerable (Pilkington et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Research on sexual trauma in men shows that disclosure and labeling oneself as a victim may violate traditional masculine norms of being strong and invulnerable <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Pilkington et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: That may have also influenced boys' reported levels of subjective distress and regret in our study.
Finally, gender differences identified in this study may also reflect gendered social meanings and consequences attached to sexual experiences.

A recent qualitative study provides insights into how seemingly similar events such as sharing a nude image, can serve very different purposes and have different social consequences depending on gender (Ringrose & Regehr, 2023).
text.formatted: A recent qualitative study provides insights into how seemingly similar events such as sharing a nude image, can serve very different purposes and have different social consequences depending on gender <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Ringrose & Regehr, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In that study, sexual double standards created victim-blaming and shaming for girls, but not for boys.
Similar processes may explain why a larger proportion of girls in the present study report regret.
This means that while comparing prevalences between boys and girls is informative, it is important to be aware that these experiences can bear different meanings and consequences.

In this study, a history of sexual abuse by an adult in offline settings was associated with substantially higher odds of having sexual experiences or being exposed to sexual violations in online settings.

Thus, Hypothesis 4 was supported, in line with the polyvictimization framework, which suggests that exposure to one form of victimization increases risk of experiencing other forms of victimization across contexts (Finkelhor et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Thus, Hypothesis 4 was supported, in line with the polyvictimization framework, which suggests that exposure to one form of victimization increases risk of experiencing other forms of victimization across contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Finkelhor et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: However, because the outcome used in this study captures a broader range of online sexual experiences, the observed continuity across offline and online contexts should be interpreted as likelihood of encountering sexualized online interactions, not solely as revictimization.
This finding also aligns with the work by Turner and colleagues (2023), who identified early offline sexual abuse as a particularly strong predictor of online sexual abuse.
text.formatted: This finding also aligns with the work by <ref type="bibr">Turner and colleagues (2023)</ref>, who identified early offline sexual abuse as a particularly strong predictor of online sexual abuse.

text.text: In their study, several forms of early life adversities were linked to increased odds of online sexual abuse, but these associations were fully mediated through risky online behaviors.
In contrast, early offline sexual abuse retained a direct effect on online sexual abuse, even when accounting for the mediating role of risky online behaviors.

This unique and direct effect may reflect lasting psychological injury that may leave children vulnerable in other contexts, also digital platforms, including distorted self-concept, distorted sense of own value, and reduced belief that one has control over one's life (Finkelhor & Browne, 1985; Turner et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This unique and direct effect may reflect lasting psychological injury that may leave children vulnerable in other contexts, also digital platforms, including distorted self-concept, distorted sense of own value, and reduced belief that one has control over one's life <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Finkelhor & Browne, 1985;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Turner et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Together, the findings by Turner and al. (2023) indicate that adolescents with history of early life adversity may benefit from digital safety education that aims to prevent risky behaviors in online settings.
text.formatted: Together, the findings by <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Turner and al. (2023)</ref> indicate that adolescents with history of early life adversity may benefit from digital safety education that aims to prevent risky behaviors in online settings.

text.text: However, youth with a history of offline sexual abuse may need to receive trauma-informed support that address broader psychosocial vulnerabilities such as distorted self-concept, self-worth and powerlessness (Finkelhor & Browne, 1985).
text.formatted: However, youth with a history of offline sexual abuse may need to receive trauma-informed support that address broader psychosocial vulnerabilities such as distorted self-concept, self-worth and powerlessness <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Finkelhor & Browne, 1985)</ref>.

text.text: The cross-sectional design of the main analyses limits conclusions about directionality.

Although sensitivity analyses adjusting for mental and somatic symptoms assessed two years earlier reduce the likelihood that the observed associations are entirely explained by pre-existing symptom differences, they do not establish temporal ordering or causality.
The associations may reflect several processes: online sexual experiences and violations may contribute to subsequent symptoms.
Alternatively, adolescents with more symptoms may be more likely to engage in sexual activities or remain in risky online settings.
Future studies should therefore use longitudinal designs, in which both online sexual experiences and symptoms are assessed repeatedly over time.

Such designs, combined with advanced statistical approaches such as random-intercept cross-lagged panel models, would make it possible to examine temporal ordering and reciprocal associations between exposure and symptoms.

Second, although the present study assessed subjective distress related to online sexual experiences and violations, as well as selected subjective appraisals such as regret or feelings of being tricked, threatened or forced into the experience, these measures captured only a limited part of the adolescents' subjective experience.

Future studies should therefore expand questionnaires with more nuanced measures that assess both contextual factors and their personal meaning such as perceived agency, consent, peer pressure or perceived social consequences, for example.
Such measures would help clarify when online sexual experiences constitute normative sexual exploration and when it becomes harmful.
Third, attrition analyses indicated that boys were less likely than girls to provide complete data on the online sexual experiences and violations items.
This differential missingness suggests that prevalence estimates, particularly among boys, should be interpreted with caution.
Similarly, among exposed youth, boys were less likely to provide ratings of subjective distress.
Future research should examine how questions about online sexual experiences and their subjective appraisals can be phrased in ways that facilitate disclosure among boys as well as girls.

Nearly half of adolescents in this population-based sample reported at least one sexual experience or violation in online settings by age 16, underscoring that digital platforms are important developmental contexts in which young people navigate sexuality, intimacy, vulnerability and potential harm.
This also suggests that such experiences are not rare or marginal events affecting a small subgroup of adolescents, but relatively common experiences.
Higher frequency of such experiences was linked to more mental and somatic health symptoms, as well as more negative subjective appraisals of these experiences.
Finally, girls, older adolescents, and individuals with a history of sexual abuse by an adult in offline settings had higher odds of reporting sexual experiences and violations in online settings.

Together, these findings underscore the need for strategies to create safer online contexts that facilitate healthy exploration and support adolescents in navigating and being conscious of the specific risks and opportunities digital platforms have.
